data.title: Apparel Stocks Gaining From Lower Sourcing Costs Like Under Armour Stock
data.description:
Bangladesh apparel exporters are under pressure as US buyers push for lower prices and tariffs squeeze factory margins, and that shift in bargaining power is starting to ripple through to US listed apparel retailers and brands. For investors, changing sourcing costs can quietly reshape earnings quality and pricing flexibility. This article walks through three stocks from our screener that appear positioned to reflect the current sourcing backdrop.

Under Armour (UAA)

Overview: Under Armour is a global sportswear company that designs and sells performance apparel, footwear and accessories for men, women and youth, mostly through wholesale partners and its own stores and e commerce. The business leans on third party manufacturing in low cost Asian hubs, which is directly relevant when sourcing costs move in favor of US apparel brands.

Operations: Under Armour generates most of its revenue in North America at about US$2.8b, with additional contributions from EMEA at about US$1.2b, Asia Pacific at about US$700 million and Latin America at about US$200 million.

Market Cap: US$2.2b

Under Armour gives you a way to consider the intersection of lower sourcing costs and a brand that is trying to repair margins and cut back on discounting. Supplier price pressure in Bangladesh and tariff refunds have supported gross margin, while management focuses on fewer SKUs, full price selling and growth in regions such as EMEA and Latin America. At the same time, the company is still working through losses, weaker footwear demand and higher tariff related costs, so any benefit from cheaper manufacturing is competing with other headwinds. For investors, the mix of a global cost base, brand reset and currently cautious sentiment raises the question of whether margin improvement and better earnings quality can outpace those risks over the next few years.

Under Armour’s margin reset story is only partly visible in the headline numbers. To see how sourcing, tariffs and brand repair are reflected in the financials, review the analysis report for Under Armour.

PVH (PVH)

Overview: PVH Corp. is a global apparel company behind Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger, designing and selling branded clothing, underwear, footwear and accessories that are produced through a wide sourcing network in low cost regions. For investors tracking the sourcing cost theme, PVH offers a direct link between factory gate prices and the economics of two global fashion brands that sell through wholesale, company stores and growing digital channels.

Operations: PVH generates most of its revenue in EMEA at about US$4.2b, followed by the Americas at about US$2.7b, APAC at about US$1.6b and licensing at about US$400 million.

Market Cap: US$3.4b

PVH provides exposure to a large scale apparel platform where sourcing costs, tariffs and pricing power all matter for how durable earnings turn out to be. The company has discussed using a broad supplier base in more than 30 countries to manage tariff headwinds, while tariff refunds and lower product costs have recently supported earnings even as regions like EMEA remained softer. At the same time, PVH continues to work through tariff related earnings pressure, a heavier reliance on legacy brands and only gradual progress in direct to consumer and e commerce. For investors interested in the US listed Apparel Retailers and Brands Benefiting from Lower Sourcing Costs theme, PVH serves as a case study in how lower FOB costs and a value signaled stock can intersect with execution risk related to tariffs, regional demand and brand relevance.

PVH’s sourcing reset and tariff workarounds could be masking a very different earnings profile than the headline story suggests. Before the next move gets priced in, read the analysis report for PVH.

V.F (VFC)

Overview: V.F Corporation is a global apparel and footwear group behind brands such as The North Face, Vans and Timberland, using mostly outsourced manufacturing in low cost Asian hubs to supply retailers and its own stores and e commerce. For this screener, V.F offers a direct way to think about how lower sourcing costs and better supplier terms could feed into the margins of established outdoor and lifestyle brands.

Operations: V.F generates most of its revenue from Outdoor at about US$5.8b, followed by Active at about US$2.7b, with a further US$1.0b reported in All Other.

Market Cap: US$5.3b

V.F presents a combination that is central to this sourcing focused screen. The company is working to improve gross margin through premiumisation, cleaner inventory and more direct to consumer sales. At the same time, outsourced manufacturing in Asia may be getting cheaper as suppliers in Bangladesh and similar markets absorb tariff pressure and rising local costs. V.F is also carrying high leverage, facing tariff headwinds and working to revive Vans and other weaker brands, so execution risk is a factor. For investors seeking exposure to lower sourcing costs tied to well known outdoor labels, V.F is a case where better cost economics, brand repair and balance sheet repair would all need to come together for the story to fully develop.

It looks like Macfarlane Group PLC (LON:MACF) is about to go ex-dividend in the next 3 days. The ex-dividend date is two business days before a company's record date in most cases, which is the date on which the company determines which shareholders are entitled to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is important as the process of settlement involves at least two full business days. So if you miss that date, you would not show up on the company's books on the record date. In other words, investors can purchase Macfarlane Group's shares before the 10th of September in order to be eligible for the dividend, which will be paid on the 8th of October.

The company's next dividend payment will be UK£0.0096 per share, and in the last 12 months, the company paid a total of UK£0.037 per share. Last year's total dividend payments show that Macfarlane Group has a trailing yield of 4.7% on the current share price of UK£0.782. Dividends are a major contributor to investment returns for long term holders, but only if the dividend continues to be paid. We need to see whether the dividend is covered by earnings and if it's growing.

Dividends are typically paid from company earnings. If a company pays more in dividends than it earned in profit, then the dividend could be unsustainable. Last year, Macfarlane Group paid out 94% of its income as dividends, which is above a level that we're comfortable with, especially if the company needs to reinvest in its business. Yet cash flow is typically more important than profit for assessing dividend sustainability, so we should always check if the company generated enough cash to afford its dividend. It distributed 32% of its free cash flow as dividends, a comfortable payout level for most companies.

It's good to see that while Macfarlane Group's dividends were not well covered by profits, at least they are affordable from a cash perspective. Still, if this were to happen repeatedly, we'd be concerned about whether the dividend is sustainable in a downturn.
